Chapter Six: Harnessing the Power of Motivation Through Timing
Have you ever noticed how your motivation isn’t always steady? Sometimes it’s high and you’re ready to take on the world, and other times, it just seems to fade away. That’s because motivation isn’t a constant force—it actually ebbs and flows, often depending on when things happen or how your day is structured.
Here’s something interesting: motivation tends to spike at specific moments. Think about how energized you feel at the start of something new—like the first day of the week, a birthday, or even the beginning of a new month. These are what we call “fresh start” moments, and they work like psychological reset buttons. They help you mentally separate any past setbacks from what’s possible ahead, making it way easier to commit to new goals or habits.
So, how can you actually use these moments to your advantage? Well, one approach is to mark new beginnings on purpose. Let’s say you want to start exercising more. Instead of picking a random day, you could begin on a Monday or after a big life event—using that sense of a new chapter to boost your commitment. Teams can do the same thing, launching new projects at the start of a quarter or a fresh phase to rally energy and set clear intentions.
Of course, as time goes on, motivation can start to dip—especially during what’s known as the “messy middle” of a project or when you’re trying to stick to a new habit. This is that point where things get tough, and it’s easy to lose steam or feel discouraged. If you know this is coming, you can plan ahead by breaking big tasks into smaller milestones and celebrating those small wins along the way. It’s a great way to keep your momentum up.
Then, as you get closer to the end of a task or a big deadline, you’ll probably notice your motivation picking up again. This “end spurt” is real, and you can harness it by setting clear deadlines and actually visualizing that finish line. Think about students who suddenly find a burst of energy right before exams, or coworkers who push extra hard as a project wraps up.
So, if you want to make the most of motivation’s natural rhythm, try these practical tips:
Start new goals or habits at meaningful “fresh start” moments. Break bigger tasks into smaller, manageable chunks—each with its own beginning and end. Celebrate your progress at key milestones to keep your enthusiasm high. And when you’re nearing the finish line, use deadlines and countdowns to create a sense of urgency and excitement.
By lining up your efforts with these natural motivational rhythms, you’ll find it’s a lot easier to stay engaged, overcome those inevitable obstacles, and keep moving toward your big goals.
